cards.cloze_text: The Claude context window is a fixed token budget that holds everything in one request at once: the {{c1::system prompt}}, the {{c2::full conversation so far}}, any {{c3::documents you inject}}, every {{c4::tool result}}, and the {{c5::model output}}.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: When estimating whether a Claude feature's cost or a given input will fit, what unit should you actually count in, and why?
cards.back: Tokens, not words or characters — tokens are the unit the API bills in and the unit the context window is measured in.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: Why is it unsafe to rely on a fixed 'N characters per token' rule of thumb when estimating token counts for Claude?
cards.back: The characters-per-token average depends on the specific model's tokenizer, and tokenizers differ between model generations — so any chars-per-token estimate is model-dependent and must be confirmed for the model actually in use, not assumed constant.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: If the input you send to Claude is already larger than the context window before generation even starts, what happens?
cards.back: The request is rejected outright with a validation error, before generation begins.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: If a request's input fits within the context window, but the model hits the token ceiling partway through generating its response, what happens?
cards.back: The model stops and returns whatever output it generated so far, with a model_context_window_exceeded stop reason — a truncated response, not a thrown error.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: Why might a Claude-based application that worked reliably throughout development suddenly start failing on the context window once it's in production?
cards.back: Development test inputs are typically short, so the window rarely fills; production sees longer inputs and more conversation turns that accumulate and fill the window faster — so keeping a long-running session working requires the application to trim or summarize history before each call.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: What does the temperature setting control when Claude generates a response?
cards.back: It shapes the probability distribution the model samples the next token from: a lower temperature concentrates probability on the most likely tokens, making output more repeatable; a higher temperature spreads probability out, making output more varied.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: What does 'non-determinism' mean for Claude's outputs, and what causes it?
cards.back: It means identical inputs do not guarantee identical outputs. It's the primary consequence of sampling: at each step the model samples the next token from a probability distribution instead of always emitting one fixed token, so wording can differ between runs even when both answers are correct.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: On the newest Claude models, what happens if you try to set a non-default temperature, top_p, or top_k?
cards.back: The API returns a 400 error — the newest models don't accept non-default sampling parameters at all; you steer their behavior through prompting instead.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: On models that accept a temperature parameter, what's the relationship between setting temperature to 0 and getting identical output across repeated calls?
cards.back: Temperature 0 makes output more repeatable, but it does not guarantee identical outputs across calls — determinism is never guaranteed, even at temperature 0.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: Since Claude's output is non-deterministic, what should a test assert on instead of the exact response text?
cards.back: The property that must actually hold — for example, that a required field is present, that a value is in range, or that the structure parses — rather than the literal wording of the response.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.front: When you need to judge whether a Claude response's meaning, not just its structure, is correct, what technique should you use?
cards.back: An eval with a model-graded judge — an evaluation that uses a model to judge whether a response's meaning meets a rubric.
cards.extra: M1 · How LLMs Behave · How LLMs behave: tokens, context, sampling, non-determinism

cards.cloze_text: Claude's model family spans four capability tiers: {{c1::Haiku}} for speed and cost efficiency, {{c2::Sonnet}} as the balanced default for most production workloads, {{c3::Opus}} for demanding work above Sonnet's envelope, and {{c4::Fable}} as the most capable tier for maximum-intelligence reasoning, coding, and agentic work.
cards.extra: M1 · Models & Reasoning · Model options and reasoning modes

cards.front: What's the practical default workflow for deciding which Claude model tier to run for a task?
cards.back: Start with Sonnet. Move up a tier only when an eval shows the current tier is missing your quality bar. Move down to Haiku only when an eval shows the resulting quality drop is acceptable for the task.
cards.extra: M1 · Models & Reasoning · Model options and reasoning modes

cards.front: A task needs more capability than Sonnet provides. What specifically distinguishes choosing Fable over Opus in that case?
cards.back: Opus handles demanding work above the Sonnet envelope; Fable is reserved as the most capable tier, for the most demanding reasoning, coding, and agentic work where maximum intelligence is the priority.
cards.extra: M1 · Models & Reasoning · Model options and reasoning modes

cards.front: Model choice and reasoning-mode choice for a Claude call — how do these two decisions relate to each other?
cards.back: They're two separate, independent decisions: model choice picks which family member runs, while the reasoning mode is a setting configured per call. The two levers are independent but compose — you can pair any model with any reasoning setting.
cards.extra: M1 · Models & Reasoning · Model options and reasoning modes

cards.front: On current Claude models, how do you control how much a model thinks before answering, now that the old approach is deprecated?
cards.back: Through adaptive thinking: the model itself decides when and how much to think, and you tune the depth with an effort setting. The older fixed budget_tokens control is deprecated and returns a 400 error on the newest model generations.
cards.extra: M1 · Models & Reasoning · Model options and reasoning modes

cards.front: By default on the newest Claude models, what does the API response include or omit regarding the model's thinking/reasoning content?
cards.back: Thinking content is omitted from the response by default — you have to explicitly request summarized display to see it.
cards.extra: M1 · Models & Reasoning · Model options and reasoning modes

cards.front: What kind of task does extended/adaptive thinking earn its cost on, and what kind of task is it wasted on?
cards.back: It earns its cost on hard, multi-step problems; it's wasted on simple lookups and classification tasks.
cards.extra: M1 · Models & Reasoning · Model options and reasoning modes

cards.front: How does pairing a smaller model with reasoning turned on compare to pairing a capable model with reasoning off?
cards.back: A capable model with reasoning off is fast and direct; a smaller model with reasoning on spends more tokens in order to think its way toward the answer.
cards.extra: M1 · Models & Reasoning · Model options and reasoning modes

cards.cloze_text: Prompting modes differ by how many worked examples accompany the instruction: {{c1::zero-shot}} gives no examples at all, {{c2::one-shot}} gives exactly one input-output example, and {{c3::multi-shot}} (also called few-shot) gives several examples.
cards.extra: M1 · Prompting Modes · Prompting modes: zero-shot, one-shot, multi-shot

cards.front: In a multi-shot prompt, what exactly are the worked example input-output pairs used for?
cards.back: They are not training data — they sit in the prompt itself and show the model the exact shape of the desired answer, which a plain description often fails to pin down.
cards.extra: M1 · Prompting Modes · Prompting modes: zero-shot, one-shot, multi-shot

cards.front: What's the decision rule for choosing among zero-shot, one-shot, and multi-shot prompting on a task?
cards.back: Reach for zero-shot when the task is simple and the output shape is obvious. Move to one-shot or multi-shot when the output has a specific structure, casing, or edge case that a description keeps missing — and add only the smallest number of examples that produces a reliable result, since each example costs tokens on every call.
cards.extra: M1 · Prompting Modes · Prompting modes: zero-shot, one-shot, multi-shot

cards.front: How can adding worked examples to a prompt let you get away with using a cheaper, smaller model for a task?
cards.back: A more capable model often succeeds zero-shot on a task where a smaller model needs a few examples to match the required output structure — so adding examples can substitute for model capability, letting a cheaper model do the job.
cards.extra: M1 · Prompting Modes · Prompting modes: zero-shot, one-shot, multi-shot

cards.front: When optimizing both model choice and prompting mode for a task, what's the recommended joint approach?
cards.back: Try the simplest model and the fewest examples that meet your eval at the same time, and add capability (a bigger model) or more examples only where the eval actually shows you need it.
cards.extra: M1 · Prompting Modes · Prompting modes: zero-shot, one-shot, multi-shot

cards.front: What's the actual relationship between an official Claude SDK (Python, TypeScript, etc.) and the raw REST API?
cards.back: The SDK is a thin convenience layer over the same REST API — it handles authentication, request construction, retries, and response parsing — but both the SDK and a raw REST call reach the exact same API and the same model. The SDK just saves you from assembling requests by hand.
cards.extra: M1 · Technical Substrate · The technical substrate: SDKs, REST, streaming, async

cards.front: When is a synchronous, wait-for-the-complete-response request pattern the right fit for calling Claude?
cards.back: For short responses and backend jobs where no one is watching in real time — you send the request, wait for the full response to come back in one piece, then act on it.
cards.extra: M1 · Technical Substrate · The technical substrate: SDKs, REST, streaming, async

cards.front: Why reach for streaming instead of a synchronous call when a user is actively watching the response arrive?
cards.back: Streaming sends the response in pieces as the model generates it, so output appears immediately instead of after a blank-screen wait, and your application code reassembles the pieces into the final message.
cards.extra: M1 · Technical Substrate · The technical substrate: SDKs, REST, streaming, async

cards.front: What underlying transport mechanism does Claude use to deliver a streamed response?
cards.back: Server-sent events (SSE), sent over the same HTTP connection used for the request.
cards.extra: M1 · Technical Substrate · The technical substrate: SDKs, REST, streaming, async

cards.front: What is AsyncAnthropic, and what problem does it solve?
cards.back: The async client exposed by the Python SDK. It uses non-blocking async/await to make API calls without tying up your application thread, while the request still returns in real time — the right pattern when you need concurrency without blocking.
cards.extra: M1 · Technical Substrate · The technical substrate: SDKs, REST, streaming, async

cards.front: In the TypeScript SDK, how do you get non-blocking, concurrent API calls — what's the equivalent of Python's AsyncAnthropic?
cards.back: There isn't a separate async client class in TypeScript — the standard Anthropic client is already Promise-based, so you just await calls directly.
cards.extra: M1 · Technical Substrate · The technical substrate: SDKs, REST, streaming, async

cards.front: What is the Message Batches API for, and what tradeoff does it make?
cards.back: A pattern for bulk offline workloads: submit a large set of requests in one call, receive an identifier, and poll for completion. It can take up to 24 hours but runs at a lower per-token cost — suited to offline pipelines, evaluation runs, and bulk jobs where no one is waiting and cost matters more than turnaround time.
cards.extra: M1 · Technical Substrate · The technical substrate: SDKs, REST, streaming, async

cards.front: AsyncAnthropic and the Message Batches API both help with high-volume work, but they solve different problems. What's the key distinction between them?
cards.back: AsyncAnthropic gives non-blocking concurrency for requests that still return in real time, so your application thread isn't tied up waiting. The Message Batches API is for genuinely offline bulk work — you submit a batch, poll for completion up to 24 hours later, and get a lower per-token cost in exchange for that latency.
cards.extra: M1 · Technical Substrate · The technical substrate: SDKs, REST, streaming, async

cards.front: A short, well-specified classification task already returns the correct answer zero-shot. What's the effect of adding three worked examples to the prompt anyway?
cards.back: It adds token cost on every call for little or no gain. Examples are for fixing a wrong output shape, not for improving a task that already works — add them only when zero-shot isn't producing a reliable result.
cards.extra: M1 · Module Wrap-up · Module quiz

cards.front: You need to process thousands of inputs completely offline, with nobody waiting on the results, and cost matters more than turnaround time. Why does a synchronous loop calling the API once per input fall short here, and what should you use instead?
cards.back: A synchronous loop at that volume hits rate limits and ties up the application. The Message Batches API is the right fit: submit the requests as a batch and poll for completion, accepting longer latency in exchange for a lower per-token cost.
cards.extra: M1 · Module Wrap-up · Module quiz

cards.front: For a classification task specifically, which temperature setting should you use, and why?
cards.back: A low temperature — it concentrates probability on the most likely tokens, so repeated runs return the same label far more consistently (though never with guaranteed determinism, even at temperature 0). A high temperature would let the label itself vary between runs, which a classifier can't afford.
cards.extra: M1 · Module Wrap-up · Exercise: predict the behavior

cards.front: For an overnight, no-user-watching job processing tens of thousands of documents, why doesn't streaming help, even though it's normally the right tool for long responses?
cards.back: Streaming's benefit is that output appears immediately for someone watching it arrive. With no user watching, that benefit buys nothing — the batch pattern (submit the requests, poll for completion, trade latency for lower per-token cost) is the right fit instead.
cards.extra: M1 · Module Wrap-up · Exercise: predict the behavior

cards.front: In a long multi-turn agent session, once the context window fills up mid-conversation, what does Claude actually do about the oldest turns?
cards.back: Nothing — the oldest turns are never silently dropped to make room. Claude either rejects an already-oversized input with an error before generation starts, or, if the ceiling is hit mid-generation, stops and returns truncated output with a model_context_window_exceeded stop reason. Trimming or summarizing history to stay within budget is the application's own responsibility.
cards.extra: M1 · Module Wrap-up · Exercise: predict the behavior
